title: Minimum Spanning Tree — Kruskal
tagline: Sort edges, add the cheapest that doesn't form a cycle — greedy MST with union-find.

intuition.analogy: Connecting towns with the least total cable: always lay the cheapest remaining cable, but skip any that would loop back to towns already linked (that cable would be wasted).
paragraphs: A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with the least total edge weight and no cycles. Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: consider edges from cheapest to most expensive and add an edge only if it joins two so-far-separate components.
Union-Find is the perfect companion: it tells you in near-constant time whether an edge's endpoints are already connected (would create a cycle). If not, union them and keep the edge.
The greedy choice is safe by the 'cut property': the cheapest edge crossing any partition of the vertices is always in some MST. Stop once you've added V−1 edges.
intuition.keyIdea: Take edges cheapest-first; add one only if its endpoints are in different DSU components.

steps.title: Sort edges by weight
steps.detail: Ascending order so you always consider the cheapest available edge next.

steps.title: Greedily add safe edges
steps.detail: For each edge (u,v,w): if find(u) ≠ find(v), union them and include the edge in the MST.

steps.title: Stop at V−1 edges
steps.detail: A spanning tree of V vertices has exactly V−1 edges; finishing early is an optimisation.

codes.source:
def kruskal(n, edges):               # edges = [(w, u, v), ...]
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    edges.sort()                     # by weight
    cost = used = 0
    for w, u, v in edges:
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru != rv:
            parent[ru] = rv
            cost += w; used += 1
            if used == n - 1:
                break
    return cost

complexity.timeReason: Dominated by sorting the edges; DSU operations are near-constant.

pitfalls: Forgetting the cycle check adds redundant edges and breaks the tree property.
Disconnected graphs have no spanning tree — detect when used < V−1.
Sort by weight, not by vertex id.

dryRun.clickMoment: The edge (2,B,C) is rejected purely because B and C already share a component. Union-Find made that O(1) check trivial — that's the marriage of greedy + DSU.

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.statement: Connect all points with minimum total Manhattan distance.
problems.hint: Build edges, Kruskal with DSU (or Prim).

approach: Build a complete graph where each edge weight is the Manhattan distance between two points, then find the MST.
Kruskal sorts all O(n^2) edges and unions endpoints with DSU, skipping edges that would form a cycle, until n-1 edges are chosen.

problems.title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
problems.statement: Minimum cost to connect all cities, or -1.
problems.hint: Kruskal; check full connectivity at the end.

approach: Classic MST: connect all cities at minimum total cost. Sort edges ascending and union endpoints with DSU.
If after processing we used fewer than n-1 edges, the graph is disconnected → return -1.

problems.title: Optimize Water Distribution
problems.statement: Minimise cost to supply water via wells or pipes.
problems.hint: Model wells as edges to a virtual node, then MST.

approach: Digging a well in a house is modelled as an edge from a virtual node 0 to that house with the well's cost.
Now every house is either connected to a neighbour by a pipe or to the 'water source' node 0. Run Kruskal on all these edges to get the cheapest way to supply water everywhere.

problems.title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges
problems.hint: Compare MST weights with each edge forced in/out.

approach: An edge is critical if removing it increases the MST weight (or disconnects the graph); pseudo-critical if it can appear in some MST but is not critical.
Compute the base MST weight. For each edge: test criticality by skipping it and rebuilding; test pseudo-criticality by forcing it in first. Sort edges but keep original indices.

problems.title: Reachability Threshold (MST-like)
problems.statement: Process edges by weight to answer connectivity queries.

approach: Offline trick: queries 'is there a path between p and q using only edges with weight < limit' are answered by adding edges in increasing weight and unioning.
Sort both edges and queries by weight/limit. Process each query after unioning all lighter edges; the answer is whether the endpoints share a DSU root.
